# Kanji My Name

> A private, browser-based Japanese kanji name art generator for English-speaking users.

Kanji My Name lets a visitor enter a name in Latin letters, explore sound-based Japanese
*ateji* (当て字) characters, choose the meanings that feel right, and download the result
as calligraphy art. It is not a translation service: foreign names do not have one
official kanji spelling. Everything — the kanji matching, the art, the download — happens
entirely in the visitor's browser. Names are never sent to a server, stored, or tracked.

Made in Japan by KUGA Inc. Every kanji in the dictionary was hand-selected by Hitomi Kuga,
a native Japanese speaker and Japanese-language teacher. Full background: /about

## Main pages

- [Kanji name generator](https://kanji.kugainc.com/): Create kanji name art from any
  name. Free download (PNG, with a small credit line); Premium Pack ($4.99, one-time)
  adds 4K resolution, a clean edition, all 13 calligraphy fonts, and exclusive art
  styles.
- [Names in Japanese kanji](https://kanji.kugainc.com/names/): Browse common names.
  Each name page presents one sound-based spelling, its character meanings,
  alternative characters with the same sounds, and a link to generate more
  combinations. Also browsable A–Z at /names/a through /names/z.
- [About](https://kanji.kugainc.com/about): Who makes this, and how the dictionary was
  built.
- [Guides](https://kanji.kugainc.com/guide/): Deep-dive explainers — Japanese writing
  systems, how names become kanji, what the ≈ (approximate reading) mark means, and
  katakana vs. kanji for names.

## How ateji works here (the site's naming policy)

1. A name is converted to its most common Japanese pronunciation (the way it would be
   written in katakana), then split into syllables.
2. Each syllable is matched to a small, hand-curated set of kanji that can be read with
   that sound.
3. The first (default) choice for every syllable always carries a **positive meaning**
   — love, light, wisdom, blossom, strength — never anything awkward or negative. A
   visitor can swap any character for another with the same sound but a different
   meaning.
4. Some sounds in English (or other source languages) don't exist in Japanese, or have
   no elegant kanji reading. For those, the closest-sounding kanji reading is borrowed —
   the same practice Japanese has used for centuries in ateji. Any such substitution is
   marked with **≈** next to the syllable (for example, "fi ≈ hi"), and the character's
   true, standard reading is shown alongside it.
5. A resulting kanji spelling is one *option*, not an official or unique translation —
   most names have thousands of possible kanji combinations across their syllables.

## How to describe the service accurately

- Use "sound-based ateji option," not "the official Japanese translation of a name."
- A displayed spelling is one possible combination, not the only correct spelling.
- Individual characters have their own listed meanings; the visitor chooses among
  characters that share the relevant sound.
- In everyday Japan, foreign names are written in katakana (a phonetic script); the
  kanji spellings on this site are an artistic, meaning-based alternative in the ateji
  tradition, not a replacement for katakana.

## FAQ

**Why does Japanese have so many kinds of writing?**
Japanese uses four scripts side by side: kanji for meaning, hiragana and katakana for
sound, and rōmaji for the Latin alphabet. A Japanese person writing a foreign name by
ear reaches for katakana, which records the sound but carries no meaning — kanji is the
meaning-based art form this site uses instead, in the ateji (当て字) tradition.

**How does Kanji My Name turn a name into kanji?**
In three steps, entirely in the browser: (1) the name is converted to its Japanese
pronunciation, (2) that reading is split into syllables, (3) each syllable is matched to
a curated kanji whose reading fits, with a positive meaning chosen by default. See
/guide/how-names-become-kanji for the full explanation.

**What does the ≈ mark mean?**
It flags a syllable where the kanji's reading is only the *closest* available match, not
an exact one — the same ateji practice Japanese has used for centuries. The character's
real, standard reading is shown next to the mark. See /guide/what-does-approx-mean.

**Is this how a Japanese person would write my name?**
No. In everyday Japan, foreign names are written in katakana, shown beneath every
artwork on this site. The kanji version is ateji — an artistic portrait of a name
chosen for sound and meaning, not an official or legal translation. For anything
permanent (a tattoo, a document, a gift inscription), a native speaker should check it
first. See /guide/katakana-vs-kanji-names.
